models.purpose: Generate child-branch directions, lengths, and three-dimensional endpoints recursively from a parent branch.
models.summary: A species-linked branch count and local rotation-scaling matrix recursively transform every parent vector; cumulative endpoints form a synthetic crown geometry.

equation_status.reason: Branch-count, transformation, vector, and endpoint equations were visually checked on pages 8-9.

objectives: Generate a spatial crown with species-linked branching geometry.
Provide branch endpoints and crown projections to downstream light and mass calculations.
constraints: The appendix implementation is binary even though the prose permits N children.
Each child is generated only from its parent vector and local parameters.
The recursion has no collision, self-intersection, or resource constraint.

details: The root vector r_1 and origin initialize the recursion.
A generation count is supplied in code, but no biological terminal rule is defined in the paper body.

parameter_estimation.method: Thirty-two candidate local coordinate orientations are compared visually for one case study; species functions and scale distributions are not fitted.

steps: Initialize the trunk vector and origin.
For each generation, select child count and local transformations.
Transform every parent vector into child vectors.
Accumulate global endpoints.
Repeat to the supplied generation count.
algorithm.convergence_criteria: The recursion stops at a user-supplied generation count; no geometric or probabilistic convergence criterion is reported.

assumptions: The tree is paracladial and subbranches preserve parent structural rules apart from size.
Local linear transformations adequately represent branch growth.
Genetic and environmental uncertainty can be compressed into parameter variation.

identifiability_feasibility.analysis: The paper supplies no objective function, parameter distributions, measured branch coordinates, or out-of-sample crown-shape loss; many parameter sets can generate visually similar profiles.

models.computational_cost: The binary appendix expands roughly as O(2^g) in generation count g; memory and runtime are not reported.
strengths: Makes the parent-child geometric handoff explicit through vectors and matrices.
Publishes MATLAB code for the main recursion.
limitations: The rounding operator in N=[theta sigma(k)] is undefined.
The general N-child prose and binary code are not reconciled.
Visual profile selection is not parameter calibration.

models.purpose: Place and orient leaves on terminal branches using a species phyllotaxis pattern, irradiance-linked spacing, and a growth probability.
models.summary: Terminal branches are identified, then leaves are assigned by one of four phyllotaxis families; two unspecified functions map irradiance to spacing and budding probability.

variables.definition: All generated branches in the vector tree.
Branches that are not parents of another branch.
Branch vector tested for membership in the terminal set.
Any branch whose parent relation is checked.
Sunlight irradiance at a candidate leaf location.
Unspecified function mapping irradiance to spacing between leaves.
Unspecified function mapping irradiance to budding probability.
Distichous, whorled, spiral, or multijugate placement rule.
Generated leaf attachment coordinates.
Generated leaf directions from the phyllotaxis rule.

governing_equations.source_expression: A={r_p in Tree | there does not exist r_k in Tree for which branch p is parent of branch k}
governing_equations.normalized_latex: A_{terminal}=\{r_p\in Tree:\nexists r_k\in Tree\text{ with parent}(k)=p\}
governing_equations.purpose: Identify the terminal branches eligible for leaf placement.

equation_status.reason: The terminal-set definition is present; the critical d(I) and p(I) response functions are named but not specified.

objectives: Generate species-consistent leaf distribution on the crown.
Link local light conditions to spacing and budding probability.
constraints: Leaves are assigned mainly to the last branch generation.
Only four botanical phyllotaxis classes are represented.
Spacing and probability functions must return physically valid values.

details: The terminal branch set from the completed vector tree is required.
No domain or range is supplied for d(I) or p(I).
The model samples a static leaf arrangement.

parameter_estimation.method: No functional form or calibration data are supplied for d(I) or p(I); the case study later assigns d(I) a normal distribution without explaining the mapping.

steps: Identify terminal branches.
Choose the species phyllotaxis family.
Use d(I) to determine spacing.
Use p(I) to sample budding sites.
Assign leaf positions and orientations.
algorithm.convergence_criteria: One placement pass is implied; no probability normalization, rejection rule, or fixed-point criterion is reported.

assumptions: Most leaves grow on terminal branches.
Species phyllotaxis and local irradiance dominate leaf position.
The light-dependent spacing and budding relations transfer across the simulated crown.

identifiability_feasibility.analysis: Without d(I), p(I), training observations, or a placement likelihood, the leaf distribution cannot be reproduced or identified from the paper.

models.computational_cost: Unreported; a direct pass over terminal branches would be linear in candidate budding sites, aside from shadow feedback.
strengths: Separates branch generation from leaf placement.
Names both a spacing mechanism and a budding-probability mechanism.
limitations: The core irradiance response functions are absent.
The later normal spacing assumption can generate negative spacing.
Leaf placement needs irradiance, while irradiance itself needs leaf geometry, creating an unresolved feedback loop.

models.purpose: Estimate directional sky brightness and integrate attenuated irradiance at a point inside the crown.
models.summary: A discretized annual solar trajectory defines a sky brightness field, while the Monsi-Saeki attenuation law uses crown path length from the vector tree to compute point irradiance over the celestial hemisphere.

equation_status.reason: The surface projection, Monsi-Saeki attenuation, and printed hemisphere integral were visually checked on pages 12-13.

objectives: Calculate local irradiance inside a generated crown.
constraints: Sun trajectories are discretized over a year.

details: The annual path is a prescribed forcing rather than a dynamic initial-value problem.
I_0 or B(theta,phi) supplies the above-crown directional boundary condition.
The model integrates a prescribed annual radiation field.

parameter_estimation.method: B(theta,phi), time weights, and k_ext are described conceptually but not numerically calibrated.

steps: Discretize the annual solar trajectory.
Accumulate absorbed radiation into B(theta,phi).
Trace each direction through the vector-tree crown to obtain s.
Apply exponential attenuation.
Numerically integrate the hemisphere.
software: Computer simulation stated; code not supplied for this integral
algorithm.convergence_criteria: No angular resolution, quadrature tolerance, or refinement test is reported.

assumptions: The solar path and sky brightness determine all incoming light.
The crown can be represented by path length and one constant extinction coefficient.

identifiability_feasibility.analysis: No measured sky brightness, path-length calibration, or within-crown irradiance data identify B or k_ext.

models.computational_cost: Proportional to time samples times angular samples times crown-ray intersection cost; no runtime is reported.
strengths: Separates directional forcing from within-crown attenuation.
Connects crown geometry to a local physical field through path length.
limitations: The printed phi changes role from azimuth to solar elevation in the surface projection.
The printed cos(theta) sin(phi) weight can be negative over the stated azimuth range.
B lacks an explicit formula and normalization.

models.family: directional shadow scoring and discrete shape selection
models.purpose: Compare candidate leaf shapes under a fixed branching structure using a sky-weighted sunlight-exposure score.
models.summary: Projected leaf shadows define a directional exposure quotient; a brightness-weighted hemisphere integral ranks four leaf-shape classes for each fixed tree profile.

algorithm.convergence_criteria: No grid refinement, angular refinement, or argmax stability test is reported.

assumptions: Observed leaf shape is selected to maximize modeled sunlight exposure.
Projected shadow is an adequate exposure proxy.
The candidate set contains a meaningful approximation to the real shape.

identifiability_feasibility.analysis: The finite ranking is executable in principle, but the appendix appears to grid branch points rather than leaf polygons and does not establish the printed score as a shadow-union area.

models.computational_cost: Roughly proportional to profiles times four shapes times angular samples times grid cells; no runtime is reported.
strengths: States the held-fixed branching structure and finite candidate comparison.
Carries directional sky weights into one normalized score.
limitations: Three profile examples are not a holdout test.
The Japanese banana scores 0.83 and 0.85 are too close to support a stable choice without uncertainty.
Summing individual shadow areas can double-count overlaps and violate the claimed [0,1] range.

limitations: The printed quadratic root omits terms and uses a sign inconsistent with the preceding equation.
No parameter table or biological-domain test is present.
The assumption that only irradiance varies is not evaluated.

parameter_estimation.method: LAI is selected from literature for Cinnamomum camphora; branch angles are chosen by visual field matching; physiological and venation parameters are not reported.

steps: Compute irradiance and P_n for each leaf.

Project the simulated crown and compute its polygon-hull ground area.

algorithm.convergence_criteria: No solver details for equations 1-4, LMA weighting rule, or projection-grid refinement criterion are reported.

identifiability_feasibility.analysis: The paper omits m_env, venation inputs, physiological parameters, and LMA weighting, and supplies no observed total leaf mass; the case-study output cannot validate the synthesis.

models.computational_cost: Per-leaf physiological calculations plus crown projection; complexity depends on leaf count, nonlinear solve details, and grid resolution, none of which are reported.
strengths: Ends with a dimensionally interpretable mass equals mass-per-area times area identity.
Connects local irradiance, leaf physiology, crown geometry, and LAI through named handoffs.
limitations: The case study reports 177.74 g/m^2 but multiplies with 177.47 g/m^2.

The individual-tree LAI and weighted-LMA procedures are unspecified.
